Alex.feeling: Tense but manageable: the table is hunting Finley over the Eagle egg count, which is useful cover, though I need to stay quiet and not get pulled into a throw.

Blair.feeling: Tense and muddled: the egg-count arguments keep going in circles, and I'm playing Meowfia while trying to stay quiet and not draw suspicion.

Casey.feeling: Messy and contradictory: Drew's and Finley's claims don't add up with the egg counts, but Ellis's confusion makes it hard to pin down who is lying.

Drew.feeling: Tense and muddled: the Eagle and Kookaburra counts don't line up, and the table is leaning toward throwing at Finley, which I can't confirm either way.

Ellis.feeling: Messy and contradictory, with conflicting Hawk and Eagle claims that nobody can cleanly resolve yet.

Finley.feeling: Tense: my Eagle count is being questioned by people who misread how the Eagle counts, and Ellis's confused report makes the table hard to read.

Alex.note: The table is converging on Finley. I'll join with a single low card so I look like the rest of the table without committing much.

Blair.note: Eggsecuting a Farm player hands Meowfia the round, so I throw at Finley with the table. Two low cards to add a vote without spending high value.

Casey.note: Finley's Eagle report still doesn't match the egg rule, and Ellis's confusion points to Finley. Throwing at Finley with two cards.

Drew.note: Blair is cleared by my Hawk visit, and Finley's Eagle report contradicts the egg count, with Ellis, Casey and Alex all leaning on it. I'm throwing two mid cards at Finley to add votes while keeping my high cards.

Ellis.note: Finley's Eagle count contradicts my confused report, and Casey and Alex are both open to Finley. I throw one low card at Finley.

Finley.note: Ellis and Casey are both pushing at me, and Ellis's confused-Kookaburra report is the least reliable claim. As Farm I'll throw two mid cards at Ellis to add a vote against the likeliest liar.

Alex.confusing: The Eagle count rule was hard to read: my Eagle visit to Blair gave +1 but the table kept debating whether the Eagle counts itself, which made Finley's +0 look suspicious for a round.
Alex.fun: Round 1, when Finley's Owl report and my Eagle visit interlocked with Casey's Falcon claim and the table converged on a throw that actually landed on the Meowfia.
Alex.change: Have the Storyteller state explicitly whether an Eagle or Owl counts its own visit, so the day isn't spent arguing over arithmetic.
Alex.regret: In round 3 I joined the throw at Finley on a weak case; I would have pressed Finley on the Eagle count earlier and kept my low card in reserve.

Blair.confusing: The Eagle's visitor count was the hardest rule to pin down, since it's unclear whether the Eagle counts itself. Several players argued about it because the dawn reports didn't make that clear.
Blair.fun: Round 3, when I was secretly Floofer, the table spent its beats arguing about Finley's Eagle count and then eggsecuted Finley, who was Farm, handing Meowfia the win. Watching the table talk itself into the wrong target was funny.
Blair.change: I'd make the dawn report state whether the Eagle counts itself, and show Kookaburra confusion more clearly, so players don't chase phantom contradictions.
Blair.regret: In round 2 I threw at Casey, who was Farm, and helped Meowfia win the round. I should have checked Drew's Hawk claim more carefully before joining the vote.

Casey.confusing: The Eagle rule was the most confusing: it wasn't clear whether an Eagle's own visit counts toward the target's visitors, and my Round 3 read depended on that. Confusion also made dawn reports unreliable, so a player could be honest and still look like a liar.
Casey.fun: Round 1 was fun: my Falcon confirmed Blair's visit to Alex, and the table's visit claims lined up around it. Watching the Owl and Eagle reports get cross-checked was the best part of the day.
Casey.change: I'd spell out the Eagle and Owl rules for self-visits and for whether a visit to yourself counts, so players aren't arguing over arithmetic. I'd also make the dawn report say explicitly when a player was confused.
Casey.regret: In Round 3 I threw at Finley, a Farm player, on an Eagle egg-count argument that was actually consistent. Knowing Alex and Blair were the Meowfia, I should have pushed the throw toward Alex or Blair instead, and I'd have kept more cards.

Drew.confusing: The Eagle counting rule was unclear: the table argued for a while over whether an Eagle counts its own visit, and that drove the round 3 vote. Dawn reports being wrong when confused also made everyone's claims hard to check.
Drew.fun: In round 2, I was Meowfia and bluffed as a Hawk, and the table turned on Casey's Falcon-to-Hawk flip, so my lie helped my side win the round. Watching everyone reason from nest counts was satisfying.
Drew.change: I would make the dawn report clearer about who visited you and whether an Eagle counts itself, so claims could be checked without argument. I would also make it explicit when two players claim the same animal in one round.
Drew.regret: In round 3 I threw two cards at Finley, who was actually Farm, because the Eagle egg math looked off; I should have checked it more carefully or thrown lower cards. Knowing Finley was Farm, I would have kept my cards and not helped the Meowfia win that vote.

Ellis.confusing: The Eagle's egg count: a visit to a player with no other visitors gave no egg, and the table argued over whether the Eagle counts itself, which made the dawn math hard to check. My own confused Kookaburra report also made my reads unreliable.
Ellis.fun: Round 2, when Casey and Drew both claimed the one Hawk and the table had to work out which claim was a lie. It was a real puzzle to unpick.
Ellis.change: Make dawn reports say explicitly what the Eagle counted and whether confusion came from a visit, so players don't have to reason out the mechanics from scratch.
Ellis.regret: In round 3 I threw at Finley, the Eagle, based on a confused report and an Eagle count I misread. I should have stayed quiet and not joined the throw, since the Eagle's visit was consistent with what I knew.

Finley.confusing: The Eagle counting rule was unclear: I first assumed an Eagle visit would always add an egg, and the table argued over whether the Eagle counts itself. Confused reports also made it hard to tell honest errors from lies.
Finley.fun: Round 1 was fun to bluff as the Sphinx: I claimed Owl and invented a Pigeon visitor, and the table spent turns trying to pin my story down.
Finley.change: I would make the dawn reports clearer about which visits count and when a confused player's information is wrong, so players can check claims more reliably.
Finley.regret: In round 3 I threw my cards at Ellis, which contributed to my own elimination; I should have kept my high cards and abstained, since Farm's votes were already going against me.

review.title: Two Hawks, One Liar
review.headline: Farm won once by catching a sloppy Owl, then lost twice to bad egg math.
review.summary: Round 1 went well for Farm. Finley's invented Owl story had a hole, and everyone threw at the Meowfia Sphinx. In round 2 two players claimed Hawk, and the table threw at the real Hawk (Casey), so Drew's Floofer won. In round 3 the table misread how the Eagle counts eggs and eggsecuted Farm Finley, so the Meowfia Alex and Blair won. Casey led from round 1 and won the game at 17.

rounds.recap: Casey's Falcon and Alex's Eagle interlocked and Blair's confusion was explained. Finley, a Sphinx bluffing Owl, said a Pigeon visited them but showed no egg. The table caught this and all five threw at Finley, a Farm win. Casey banked 14 points.

Drew, a Floofer, claimed Hawk. Casey, the real Hawk, had also claimed Falcon at first by mistake. The table treated Casey's role slip as the lie and ignored the double Hawk claim. Casey was eggsecuted, a Meowfia win, though only Drew scored for it (0 points, wilds thrown).

Both Meowfia (Sphinx Alex, Floofer Blair) stayed quiet. Casey wrongly said Finley's Eagle should have gained an egg, and Ellis's confused report fed the pile-on. Everyone but Finley threw at Finley, a Farm player, and the Meowfia won. Blair banked 8.

highlights.text: Finley, the Sphinx, invented a Pigeon visitor for a made-up Owl, and Blair, Casey, Drew and Ellis all spotted that no egg fit.
Drew claimed the same Hawk as Casey, and the table threw at the true Hawk because of her earlier Falcon slip.
Ellis's confused Kookaburra report was used as proof against Finley, who was telling the truth.
Alex and Blair, both Meowfia and unaware of each other, said almost nothing and let Farm eggsecute a Farm player.

confusions.what: Called herself Falcon at first, then Hawk in the same round, which cost her the vote.
Said Blair's Eagle should have gained an egg from visiting Ellis. The Eagle only counts other visitors.
Repeated the Eagle error against Finley, then doubted Blair's correct reading.
Backed the wrong Eagle math, even though Alex was Meowfia and it helped the cover.
Claimed a Pigeon visited the Owl but no egg arrived. A Pigeon lays an egg in the target's nest.
Said the Kookaburra report showed no role for Drew. The report was empty, which the table never explained.
Used a confused report as proof that someone visited. Confusion only changes what you are told, and Ellis's confusion was caused by Finley's visit, so this was just inference.
Said Casey cannot be Hawk since Drew already claimed it. This is a bluff, but nobody asked whose claim came first.
Stated that a Kookaburra gets confused when visited. That was correct, but Alex had no reason to know it.

worked: Round 1 Owl bluff: a claim whose results could be checked against egg tokens was caught by the table. Cross-checking worked.
Two players claiming one unique animal (Hawk, round 2) is a clean contradiction, and the Meowfia bluff there was a real gamble.
Throw count and the consolation rule gave real choices. Casey threw three cards at Drew in round 2 and got H12 back.
problems: Egg-token math is easy to misread, and the Eagle not counting itself was argued in two rounds. Add an Eagle example to the rules, or have the app state the visitor count plainly.
Confusion makes reports useless but players treated them as evidence. Ellis's Kookaburra and Blair's Kookaburra stalled the day. Make confusion visible to the table.
Meowfia who do not know each other mostly went silent and won by letting Farm err. The Meowfia have little to do, and in round 3 they never had to bluff. Give them a visible way to act.
Casey's 17 after round 1 (13s banked) made the rest of the game feel decided. A catch-up rule or a lower top value would help.
Mouser, House Cat and Sphinx never made a real difference. Sphinx only revealed Drew as Hawk, and nobody was winked or killed. Wink needs a stronger role.
